articles.title: Sweden’s Critical Minerals: Why Its Rare Earths Have No Mine Yet - Discovery Alert
articles.summary: Sweden’s Critical Minerals: Why Its Rare Earths Have No Mine Yet  Discovery Alert
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- LKAB lifted the Per Geijer resource to about 1.3 billion tonnes of iron and phosphorus, containing about 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides, up from about 1.7 million tonnes.
- The Per Geijer rare earth component is only an Inferred Mineral Resource under PERC 2021, the lowest-confidence category, so it cannot be treated as a reserve or a producing mine.
- Swedish mines produced just under 80 million tonnes of ore in 2025, and Sweden supplies about 8% of EU copper, 42% of EU lead and 36% of EU zinc, but no rare earths.
- LKAB's ReeMAP, covering Malmberget and Per Geijer with processing at Luleå, won EU Strategic Project status in March 2025, which speeds permitting but does not guarantee a mine.
- Lithium, cobalt and nickel in Sweden remain occurrences and exploration targets, with no producing lithium mine or current lithium reserve found.
Sweden has one of Europe’s largest reported rare earth deposits, at roughly 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides. Yet no Swedish mine is producing rare earths today. That gap between a headline tonnage and an actual operating mine is the most useful thing to understand about Sweden’s critical minerals story.
Most Swedish mining takes place in the Baltic Shield, also called the Fennoscandian Shield. It is the oldest rock in Europe and has supplied iron and base metals for more than a century.
The European Union’s critical raw materials policy has now turned attention to what else that bedrock might hold. Rare earths, lithium, cobalt and nickel all appear in Swedish geological surveys, and each one sits at a different stage of proof.
This explainer gives you a way to read any Swedish critical mineral headline. It covers where the rock comes from, what is actually mined, and what each classification label really tells you.
Why does the Baltic Shield host so much metal?
Start with the age. The Fennoscandian Shield is Precambrian crystalline bedrock, meaning old, hard rock formed before complex life appeared. Sweden’s main ore regions sit in the Svecokarelian orogen, a mountain-building belt formed roughly 2.0-1.8 billion years ago.
That belt was built through a long sequence of events: volcanic arcs, magma intrusions, folding, heating under pressure and later hot-fluid activity. The volcanic and intrusive rocks supplied the metals. The faults and altered zones gave mineral-rich fluids a path to travel and concentrate.
The Geological Survey of Sweden (SGU) names three principal ore districts in its 2026 National Exploration Programme: Northern Norrbotten, the Skellefte district and Bergslagen. Each district carries a different metal signature because a different part of that ancient sequence dominated there.
According to SGU, five features make the shield favourable:
- Volcanic arcs and submarine basins suited to sulphide deposits
- Intrusive and volcanic systems suited to iron-oxide-apatite deposits
- Long-lived deformation zones that moved and concentrated metals
- Widely exposed bedrock, which makes mapping and exploration easier
- Established infrastructure and processing expertise built around iron and sulphide mining
Iron-oxide-apatite deposits of Norrbotten
Kiruna, Malmberget, Svappavaara and Per Geijer are Kiruna-type iron-oxide-apatite deposits. They are dominated by magnetite or hematite, both iron oxides, alongside apatite, a mineral that contains phosphorus.
Apatite is the link to the critical minerals conversation. It can host rare earth elements, so iron mines in this setting carry potential by-product value beyond iron itself.
Your reading of Swedish headlines gets sharper once you separate rare metals and rare earths, because the two groups differ in extraction methods, supply chains and market behaviour, and a label like ‘critical’ can cover very different materials.
Volcanogenic massive sulphides of the Skellefte district
The Skellefte district is dominated by volcanogenic massive sulphide (VMS) deposits. These form when hot fluids from submarine volcanoes deposit metals on or below the seafloor, and here they mainly carry zinc, copper and lead with gold and silver.
Academic work places many of these deposits around the transition between the volcanic Skellefte Group and the overlying Vargfors Group. That boundary is the favourable setting explorers look for.
Key point: Geology creates prospectivity, not automatic economic supply.
You should read the shield’s age and structure as a reason to investigate Sweden’s critical mineral potential. Prospectivity says nothing yet about tonnage, grade or economics.

What does Sweden actually mine today?
Before weighing potential, it helps to see what the districts already deliver. According to SGU figures published in June 2026, Swedish mines produced just under 80 million tonnes of ore in 2025, roughly unchanged from 2024.
Iron ore output rose slightly. Base metal and gold production fell, while silver rose.
That output gives Sweden real weight in Europe. SGU reports Sweden’s share of EU production as:
- Approximately 8% of EU copper
- Approximately 42% of EU lead
- Approximately 36% of EU zinc
The table below draws only on dated, sourced figures. Where no mine-specific 2025 figure was found, it says so.
| District or mine | Main commodity | Geological setting | Latest dated production information | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Kiruna (LKAB) | Iron ore | Iron-oxide-apatite | No mine-specific 2025 figure found | 
| Malmberget (LKAB) | Iron ore | Iron-oxide-apatite | Cumulative production about 640 million tonnes (SGU, 2026) | 
| Aitik (Boliden) | Copper, gold, silver | Porphyry copper | About 41 million tonnes of ore in 2023; about 1.03 billion tonnes cumulative, 1968-2023 | 
| Kristineberg, Renström, Kankberg (Boliden area) | Zinc, copper, lead, gold, silver | VMS, Skellefte district | No mine-specific 2025 figures found | 
| Garpenberg (Boliden) | Polymetallic sulphides | Bergslagen | No mine-specific 2025 figure found | 
Aitik shows why districts like these endure. A mine that started in 1968 passed a billion tonnes of cumulative production by 2023, helped by shared infrastructure, processing knowledge and continued resource work. The Boliden processing plant also treats ore from several Skellefte mines, which lets smaller, complex deposits keep operating.
You can use this as your benchmark. When a critical mineral project is described, compare its status with the decades of operating history behind these districts.
What is the difference between an occurrence, a resource and a mine?
Every mineral figure belongs to a rung on a classification ladder. Reporting codes such as JORC (Australia’s Joint Ore Reserves Committee Code) and the PERC Reporting Standard 2021, the European code referenced for current Swedish reporting, define what each rung means.
| Term | Meaning | What it does not prove | 
|---|---|---|
| Mineral occurrence | Documented presence of a mineral or raised element level | Tonnage, continuity, economic grade or mineability | 
| Historic estimate | Older estimate, often under a former code | May not qualify as a current compliant resource | 
| Inferred Resource | Lowest-confidence resource category | Cannot normally be treated as a reserve | 
| Indicated Resource | Enough confidence to evaluate mine planning | Still needs economic, legal, environmental and technical success | 
| Measured Resource | Highest-confidence resource category | Still not automatically a mine | 
| Ore Reserve | Economically mineable part of a Measured or Indicated Resource | Financing, permits or construction | 
| Producing mine | Permitted operation mining and processing ore commercially | That production cannot be suspended or become uneconomic | 
Climbing from the bottom to the top means passing a series of separate tests:
- Exploration: drilling shows continuity, grade and volume.
- Resource modelling: the data supports a compliant classification.
- Metallurgy: the valuable minerals can be recovered at acceptable cost.
- Engineering: mining, water, waste and infrastructure plans work.
- Economics: prices, costs and financing support the project.
- Permitting: environmental, land-use, water, heritage and mining approvals are granted.
- Construction and commissioning: the mine and plant operate reliably and production is sustained.
Worked examples: Per Geijer and Norra Kärr
According to its 2025 resource report, LKAB lifted the iron and phosphorus resource at Per Geijer, near Kiruna, to about 1.3 billion tonnes, containing about 2.2 million tonnes of rare earth oxides in situ. SGU’s September 2025 newsletter reported the rare earth figure rising from about 1.7 million tonnes. The rare earth component is an Inferred Mineral Resource under PERC 2021, and it sits beside existing mining infrastructure.
Correct wording: “reported inferred Mineral Resource”, not “producing rare earth mine”.
Norra Kärr in Småland tells a different story. A 2021 preliminary economic assessment was based on about 110 million tonnes at about 0.5% total rare earth oxides, but no current compliant classification was found in the material reviewed. Its earlier mining lease was revoked, a new concession application went in during December 2024, and a final decision remained outstanding in the sources found.
Other rare earth occurrences confirmed by SGU chemical analyses stay occurrences unless a compliant statement supports them. Before drawing any conclusion, ask which rung a number sits on.
Sweden is not alone in this pattern; Argentina’s rare earth gap shows another jurisdiction with large identified and modelled oxide tonnage but zero commercial production, where the barrier is legal rather than geological.
Where do lithium, cobalt, nickel and EU policy fit in?
The ladder is tidy. The real picture is messier, because policy designation, geology and actual status can each point in a different direction.
